name: Heaps and Priority Queues
intent: Know what a heap guarantees and what it does not: cheap access to the smallest item, an O(n) build, top-k without sorting, why decrease-key needs a position index, and how a strict-priority scheduler starves low-priority work.
scenario: A job scheduler keeps its tasks in an array and scans for the most urgent one on every tick. With 10,000 tasks that is 50,015,000 steps to push and pop them all, against 239,300 with a heap. A report wants the 100 biggest orders out of 10,000 and uses a heap of 100, which is fast on shuffled data and slower than a plain sort on data that arrives in ascending order. And a priority-9 job has waited since tick 0 because something more urgent always arrives.
problem: A priority queue answers one question, 'what is the most urgent item?', and a binary heap answers it cheaply by keeping only a partial order. That bargain has edges. The array is not sorted, so you cannot iterate it in order or search it. Updating a priority needs to find the item first. The top-k trick depends on how many items get in. And a queue that always serves the most urgent item is unfair by construction, which scheduling has to repair on purpose.

howItWorks.title: A tree in an array that keeps only the smallest on top
howItWorks.text: A binary min-heap stores a complete binary tree in a flat array: the children of position i are at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and every parent is no larger than its children. That is all it promises: the smallest item is at position 0, and the rest is only partly ordered. Push appends the item at the end and lets it climb past larger parents (sift up, at most log2 n levels). Pop takes the root, moves the last item to the root and lets it sink, comparing with the smaller child at each level (sift down, about two comparisons per level). Against an unsorted array (cheap push, a scan on every pop) and a sorted array (cheap pop, shifting on every push), a heap makes both cost about log n: n pushes and n pops need 17,194 steps for 1,000 items where the unsorted array needs 501,500 and the sorted array 246,079.

howItWorks.title: Building a heap is O(n), not n log n
howItWorks.text: If you already hold all the items, pushing them one at a time costs up to n log n: 113,631 comparisons for 10,000 items in descending order, because each new item is the smallest and climbs all the way. Bottom-up heapify instead sifts down every parent, starting from the last one, and costs under 2n comparisons whatever the order: 19,982 in that same case. It is cheap because half of the nodes are leaves and need no work, a quarter can sink at most one level, an eighth at most two, and the sum of those levels stays proportional to n. That is one of the few places where a log n structure builds in linear time.

howItWorks.title: Top-k with a heap of size k
howItWorks.text: To keep the k largest of a stream, keep a min-heap of k items. Compare each new item with the root (the smallest kept): if it is not larger, drop it for one comparison; otherwise replace the root and sift down, at most log2 k levels. That is about n log k, and for 10 of 10,000 shuffled items it costs 10,285 comparisons against 120,463 for sorting everything. It also uses memory for k items only and works on a stream you cannot store. The edges: the gain disappears as k grows, and on adversarial order every item enters the heap. With 100 of 10,000 items in ascending order the heap needs 123,566 comparisons, more than a merge sort of shuffled data (120,463), and a merge sort of the ascending data itself is cheaper still. The heap holds the k items unordered; putting them in order costs another k log k.

howItWorks.title: Decrease-key: the heap cannot find an item
howItWorks.text: Shortest-path search and schedulers lower the priority of an item that is already queued. The array is only partly ordered, so finding the item means scanning it. Three ways out: keep a position index (a second array or map from item to its place, updated on every swap) and sift up from there, costing 17,707 comparisons in all for 1,000 updates plus a full drain; scan for the item first, 684,633 steps for the same work; or lazy duplicates, which push a new entry with the new priority and skip the stale one when it surfaces, 37,818 comparisons but a heap that grew to 2,000 entries for 1,000 items. Standard library queues typically offer only push and pop, so the lazy approach is the common one, and a position index is what you build when the extra memory or the extra pops start to matter.

howItWorks.title: Scheduling: strict priority starves
howItWorks.text: A scheduler that always serves the most urgent task is easy to build with a heap and unfair by design: if more urgent work keeps arriving at the rate it is served, the priority-9 task that arrived first never runs (in the model, not within 2000 ticks). Aging repairs it: make the queue key the priority times a weight plus the arrival time, so every task gains one level for each stretch of waiting. The same task is then served at tick 43 with 10 ticks per level. The weight is the policy: a large one is nearly strict priority, a small one approaches first come first served. Equal priorities also need a tie-break such as a sequence number, because a heap does not keep equal items in arrival order.

pros: Push and pop both cost about log2 n comparisons, so interleaving them stays cheap
Builds from existing data in under 2n comparisons
Top-k needs memory for k items only, and works on streams
A flat array: no pointers, good memory locality, and simple to implement correctly
cons: Only the minimum is cheap to read: the array is not sorted, and finding or removing an arbitrary item is O(n) without an index
Does not keep equal priorities in arrival order
Decrease-key needs a position index or lazy duplicates, which cost memory or extra pops
Strict priority order can starve low-priority work
whenToUse: Always taking the next most urgent item while new items keep arriving: schedulers, timers, event simulations, merging many sorted streams
The k best of a large or unbounded stream, with k small against n
Dijkstra-style and A*-style searches that repeatedly take the closest unvisited node
Building a priority queue from a batch you already hold
whenNotToUse: You need the whole sequence in order: sort once instead
You need to look up, update or remove arbitrary items often: use a map plus an indexed heap, or an ordered tree
k is a large fraction of n, where a heap saves little over a sort
A queue with fixed, few priority levels: one FIFO queue per level is simpler and keeps arrival order
pitfalls: Treating the heap array as sorted: reading it left to right gives the root first and then an order that is only loosely related to priority; to get items in order you must pop them one at a time
Building a heap with n pushes when you hold all the data: 113,631 comparisons for 10,000 descending items against 19,982 for bottom-up heapify

Reaching for a heap of size k when k is large or the input is adversarial: 100 of 10,000 items in ascending order costs 123,566 comparisons, more than a merge sort of shuffled data (120,463), let alone of the already ascending data

Using the wrong kind of heap for top-k: the k largest need a min-heap of size k, whose root is the smallest of the kept items; in a library that only has a min-heap, negate the keys to keep the k smallest
Assuming equal priorities come out in arrival order: heaps are not stable, so add a sequence number to the key (the model uses the task's id)

Changing the priority of an item that is already in the heap without telling the heap: the invariant breaks silently and later pops come out in the wrong order; remove and re-insert, or sift from a known position
Finding an item by scanning before decrease-key: 684,633 steps for 1,000 updates against 17,707 with a position index
Lazy duplicates without bounds: the heap grew to 2,000 entries for 1,000 items, and every pop must check whether the entry is stale
Serving strictly by priority with no aging: a task with priority 9 never ran within 2000 ticks while more urgent work kept arriving

roles.label: Producer
roles.description: Adds items with a priority, one by one or as a batch.

roles.label: Heap
roles.description: A partly ordered array with the most urgent item at position 0.

roles.label: Consumer
roles.description: Takes the most urgent item each time it is free.

roles.label: Position index
roles.description: Remembers where each item sits, so its priority can change.

roles.label: Scheduler
roles.description: Chooses the key, such as priority plus aging, that the heap orders by.

quiz.question: You already hold 10,000 items and need them in a heap. Which approach needs the fewest comparisons?
options: Push them one at a time, which is bounded by about n comparisons in total.
Sort them first with a merge sort, since a sorted array is a valid heap and sorting is cheap.
Sift down each parent from the last one up, which takes under 2n comparisons.
Pop them from an empty heap in turn, since the heap decides the order itself.
quiz.explanation: Bottom-up heapify costs under 2n comparisons whatever the order: 19,982 for the descending case. One-by-one pushes cost up to n log n (113,631 there), and sorting first costs about n log n as well. Popping from an empty heap is not possible.

quiz.question: A top-100 query runs over 10,000 items that arrive in ascending order, using a heap of size 100. How does it compare with sorting all 10,000?
options: No better: every item beats the smallest kept one and sifts down, so it costs as much as sorting.
Far better: one comparison with the root rules out each item, whatever the order.
Far worse: the heap must be rebuilt from scratch whenever a new item arrives.
It cannot run: a heap cannot take input that is already in ascending order.
quiz.explanation: In ascending order each new item is larger than everything kept, so it replaces the root and sinks about log2 100 levels. That costs 123,566 comparisons here against 120,463 for a merge sort of shuffled data (a merge sort of the ascending input needs fewer). On shuffled data most items are dropped after one comparison, which is why the heap usually wins.

quiz.question: A shortest-path search lowers the priority of an item already in a heap, and the heap has no position index. What do library-based implementations typically do?
options: Binary-search the heap for the item, since the array is sorted.
Edit the priority in place and skip the sift, since the heap repairs itself on pop.
Rebuild the whole heap after every change, which is cheaper than any alternative.
Push a second entry with the new priority and ignore the stale one when it surfaces.
quiz.explanation: A heap is not sorted, so it cannot be binary searched, and editing in place breaks the invariant. Pushing a duplicate and skipping stale entries needs no index, at the cost of a bigger heap: 37,818 comparisons and 2,000 entries for 1,000 items, against 17,707 with an index.
